translations.title: The Cut-Off Time Question: What A Warehouse Actually Commits To And How To Test It
translations.excerpt: Every warehouse publishes a cut-off time and almost none define it the same way. The gap between the stated hour and the orders that actually leave the building is where your delivery promise quietly breaks.
translations.coverAlt: Loading dock at dusk with a wall clock visible above the outbound door and a parcel conveyor feeding a waiting trailer,
translations.metaTitle: Warehouse Cut-Off Time: What It Covers And How To Test
translations.metaDescription: A published cut-off time is a promise about which orders ship today. Learn what the promise excludes, which questions expose a soft commitment, and how to test it with live orders.
translations.content:
A cut-off time is a commitment that orders received before a stated hour ship the same working day. Ask what counts as received, which order types are excluded, how holidays and inbound backlogs change it, and where the timestamps come from. Then test it with real orders before you rely on it.

  • A cut-off time only means something once the warehouse defines what counts as an order being received.
  • Most cut-off disputes come from excluded order types, not from the stated hour itself.
  • The carrier pickup schedule, not the packing bench, usually sets the real ceiling on same day shipping.
  • Holiday calendars in the United States and Mexico do not overlap, and a shared cut-off has to name both.
  • A cut-off that cannot be measured from system timestamps is a sales statement, not an operating commitment.

What does a cut-off time actually promise?

It promises that orders meeting a defined set of conditions before a stated hour will be handed to a carrier the same working day, and everything outside those conditions is unpromised.

A cut-off time looks like a simple number on a proposal. In practice it is a conditional statement with four parts, and only one of them is the hour. The other three are the definition of a received order, the list of order types the commitment covers, and the calendar it runs on. Warehouses that operate well can state all four without hesitation. Warehouses that have never been pressed on it give you the hour and stop there. Start with the definition of received. Does the clock start when the shopper completes checkout, when your order management system releases the order, when the warehouse system creates the record, or when the pick list is generated? These moments can sit far apart. If your integration pushes orders in scheduled batches, an order placed twenty minutes before the stated hour may not exist in the warehouse system until after it. The warehouse will report full compliance and your customer will still wait an extra day. Next comes coverage. Almost every cut-off excludes something: multi item orders above a certain size, orders requiring assembly or kitting, orders with serialized products, hazardous goods, orders flagged for address verification, and first orders from a new SKU that has not been received and put away. None of these exclusions are unreasonable. The problem is when they are discovered after the first busy week rather than named in advance. The fourth part is the calendar. Working day is not a universal term. Ask which days count, how weekends are handled, and which holiday calendar applies. For a route that starts in the United States and ends in Mexico, both calendars matter and they do not line up. A commitment that names only one country will silently fail on the days when the other side is closed, and those days are usually the ones with the heaviest order volume behind them. Write all four parts into one sentence and read it back to the warehouse. If the sentence is uncomfortable to say out loud, it is not a commitment yet. If they can say it plainly and add the exceptions themselves before you ask, you are talking to an operation that has already been held to this standard by another customer.

Why do published cut-off times and real ship times drift apart?

Because the constraint is usually the carrier pickup schedule and the inbound workload, not the speed of picking and packing.

The most common misunderstanding about cut-off times is that they measure how fast a warehouse works. They do not. They measure whether the building can finish an order before the truck leaves. A parcel packed quickly and left on the outbound dock after the carrier has departed is, from the customer's point of view, an order that did not ship. The packing bench was never the constraint. That means the first question about drift is a scheduling question. When does each carrier pick up, and is that a fixed appointment or a variable window? Does the warehouse hold a later drop off option at a carrier facility, and does it use that option for delayed orders or only for exceptions? A building with a single early pickup and an ambitious published cut-off is making a promise it can only keep on light days. The second cause of drift is inbound workload. Receiving and outbound compete for the same people. When a container arrives, or when a supplier sends an unannounced delivery, put away work absorbs the staff who would otherwise be picking. Ask how the warehouse prioritizes when both queues are full, whether outbound is protected, and what happens to your orders on the days a large inbound lands. The honest answer is usually that something gives, and you want to know what. The third cause is exception handling. An order that cannot be picked cleanly leaves the flow and waits for a human decision. Missing stock at the pick face, a damaged unit, a barcode mismatch, a returned item that has not been made sellable again. Each of these pulls an order out of the same day queue. Ask what share of orders becomes an exception and how long an exception waits before someone touches it. That number describes the warehouse under stress better than any average. The fourth cause is seasonal. Mexican retail volume rises sharply in specific periods, and a warehouse that looks clean in a quiet month may behave differently when volume doubles. Ask for data from a previous peak, ask whether the cut-off changed during that period, and ask which order types were pulled out of the commitment. The answer tells you what your own peak will look like, which is the only version of the cut-off that will ever matter to your customers.

Which questions expose a soft cut-off before you sign?

Questions about measurement, exclusions and failure handling, because a soft cut-off cannot survive being asked where the numbers come from.

There is a short list of questions that separates a real operating commitment from a marketing line. Ask them in one sitting and take notes on how quickly the answers arrive. Hesitation is data. The first question is where the compliance number comes from. If it is produced from warehouse system timestamps for every order in the period, you can work with it. If it is assembled by hand for the meeting, it describes what someone remembers. The second question is about distribution rather than average. Ask for the share of eligible orders that shipped the same working day across a full recent month, not a selected week, and ask to see the worst days separately. Every operation has bad days. What matters is whether the warehouse can explain them without being asked twice, and whether the explanation points to something they have since changed. The third question is about exclusions in reverse. Instead of asking what is covered, ask which orders were not counted in the compliance number. This phrasing is harder to deflect. It surfaces the quiet carve outs: orders released after an internal deadline, orders with a hold flag, orders for SKUs still in receiving, orders that arrived through a channel with a slower feed. The fourth question is about failure. What happens when a covered order misses the cut-off? Does anyone notice automatically, does the warehouse tell you before you discover it in a tracking page, and is there a defined action such as upgrading the service level at the warehouse's cost? A commitment without a defined failure path is a preference. Ask to see an example from the last month, including the message that was sent to the customer. The fifth question is about change control. Cut-off times move. Staffing changes, carriers reschedule pickups, a new customer with heavy volume arrives in the same building. Ask how much notice you get before the cut-off changes, in what form, and whether it can change temporarily without notice during peak. Then ask for that notice period in writing. This single clause prevents most of the unpleasant surprises that show up two quarters into a relationship, usually in the middle of your best selling week.

How do you test a cut-off time with live orders?

Place your own orders at deliberate times over several weeks, record the timestamps at every handoff, and compare them with the warehouse report.

Testing a cut-off is straightforward and almost nobody does it. The method is to place real orders through your own storefront at chosen times and follow them end to end. Place one well before the stated hour, one shortly before it, one just after it, and one late in the evening. Repeat the pattern on a Monday, on a Friday, and on a day when you know an inbound delivery is scheduled. The pattern matters more than the volume. For each test order, record four timestamps: the checkout confirmation, the order record creation in the warehouse system, the ship confirmation, and the first carrier scan. The gap between ship confirmation and first carrier scan is the most revealing of the four. A ship confirmation issued at the cut-off followed by a carrier scan the next morning tells you the label was created on time and the parcel was not. That distinction is invisible in most reports. Vary the order types as well. Include a multi item order, an order with a heavier product, an order to a residential address in a smaller city, and an order for a SKU that arrived recently. If any of these behave differently, you have found an exclusion that was not on the list. Note it, raise it, and get the answer added to the written definition before you scale volume. Run the test across several weeks rather than several days. A single week can be flattering or unlucky. Weeks that include a holiday on either side of the border are especially useful, because they show whether the calendar question was answered honestly. Keep the results in a simple sheet with one row per order, because the sheet is what makes the conversation with the warehouse concrete instead of anecdotal. When you compare your sheet with the warehouse compliance report, expect a difference and treat it as the start of a discussion rather than an accusation. Most differences come from definitions, not from dishonesty. The value of the exercise is that it forces both sides to agree on which timestamp starts the clock. Once that is settled, the number on the proposal finally means the same thing to you and to the people packing your orders.

What should the written agreement say about cut-off and exceptions?

It should name the hour, the definition of a received order, the covered order types, both holiday calendars, the reporting source and the notice period for changes.

Once the questions are answered and the test is done, put the result into the agreement. This is not about creating leverage for a dispute. It is about making sure the person who runs the floor next year works from the same definition as the person who sold you the service this year. Staff changes on both sides, and written definitions outlast them. Start with the sentence you built earlier: which orders, received by when, measured how, ship on which days. Add the exclusion list explicitly, including the order types that were discovered during testing. Exclusions in writing are not a weakness in the relationship. They are the difference between a warehouse that meets a narrow promise reliably and one that misses a broad promise regularly. Add the reporting clause next. Name the source system, the frequency, the fields, and the fact that the report covers every order in the period rather than a sample. Ask for the raw order level export alongside the summary. A summary tells you whether the month was good. The export tells you which days and which order types were not, which is the only version you can act on. Include a change notice clause. Specify how far in advance the warehouse tells you about a permanent change to the cut-off or the carrier pickup schedule, and how it communicates temporary changes during peak. Also specify who at your company receives that notice, because a message sent to an inbox nobody reads is the same as no message. Keep the recipient list current. Finally, agree on a short review rhythm. A monthly conversation with a fixed agenda works better than an escalation call after a bad week. Look at same day performance, the exceptions that took longest, the days that failed and the reason, and any change to the calendar ahead. Regulations affecting import steps and product labeling sit outside this conversation and should be handled with a qualified specialist, but the operating commitment itself belongs in this review, in writing, and in language both sides can read the same way.

Hard cut-off versus soft cut-off

What you askHard cut-offSoft cut-off
What counts as receivedWarehouse system record creation, defined in writingRoughly when the order comes in
Covered order typesNamed list with exclusions stated up frontStandard orders, exceptions handled case by case
CalendarWorking days named, both US and Mexican holidays listedBusiness days, holidays handled as they arise
Reporting sourceOrder level export from warehouse system timestampsSummary prepared for the review meeting
Missed order handlingAutomatic alert, defined action, customer notifiedDiscovered by the seller in the tracking page

How BringGo Ship handles cut-off commitments

BringGo Ship moves goods from the United States into Mexico through our own warehouses in Laredo, Texas and Monterrey, Mexico. We tell you at the start what our cut-off hour is, which moment we treat as the order being received, which order types fall outside the commitment, and how our schedule changes around holidays on both sides of the border. We measure performance from the timestamps our warehouse system records rather than from a report assembled by hand, and we share the order level detail with you, not only the monthly summary. When an order that should have shipped does not, we tell you before you find it in a tracking page. We support customers in English, Spanish and Turkish, so the person reviewing these numbers with you works in your own language. For import procedure and product labeling questions we point you to a qualified specialist and stay focused on the operational commitments we can measure.

Definitions

  • Cut-off time: The last hour at which a warehouse accepts orders for handling on the same working day.
  • Handling time: The interval between an order appearing in the warehouse system and the parcel being handed to a carrier.
  • Ship confirmation: The system event that marks an order as dispatched, which is not the same as the parcel physically leaving the building.
  • Exception order: An order that leaves the normal flow and waits for a human decision, such as a pick shortage or a barcode mismatch.

Frequently asked questions

Is a ship confirmation the same as a shipped parcel?

No. A ship confirmation is a system event that creates a label and updates the channel. The parcel has shipped when the carrier takes physical custody and produces the first scan.

Which is more important, the cut-off hour or the exclusions?

The exclusions. Most disputes come from order types nobody named in advance rather than from the hour itself, so ask which orders were left out of the compliance number.

How long should a cut-off test run?

Long enough to cover several weeks, including a Monday, a Friday, a day with a large inbound delivery, and at least one week containing a holiday on either side of the border.

Why do US and Mexican holiday calendars matter for one cut-off?

Because the route uses both. A commitment that names only one calendar fails quietly on the days when the other side is closed, usually with a backlog behind it.

What should I do if my test results differ from the warehouse report?

Treat it as a definition problem first. Compare which timestamp each side uses to start the clock, then agree on one source and restate the commitment around it.

translations.excerpt: Pedimento, Meksika'ya yapılan her ticari ithalatın zorunlu gümrük beyannamesidir. Nedir, nasıl okunur, süreç nasıl işler ve ne kadara mal olur: hepsini net anlatıyoruz.

translations.metaDescription: Pedimento, Meksika ithalatının zorunlu gümrük beyannamesidir. Nedir, hangi alanları taşır, süreç nasıl işler ve maliyeti nedir: güncel 2026 rehberi.
translations.content:
Pedimento, Meksika'ya yapılan her resmi ithalat ve ihracatın elektronik gümrük beyannamesidir. Malın değerini, tarife kodunu, menşeini, ödenen vergileri ve lisanslı gümrük müşavirinin bilgilerini taşır. Ticari ithalatta bu beyanı yalnızca kayıtlı bir gümrük müşaviri (agente aduanal) sunabilir. Kısacası pedimento olmadan mal Meksika sınırından yasal olarak geçemez.

  • Pedimentoyu yalnızca lisanslı gümrük müşaviri (agente aduanal) sunabilir; 2026 gümrük reformu bunu değiştirmedi (QIMA, White & Case).
  • 2026 reformuyla ithalatçı ve müşavir beyandaki bilgiden ortak sorumludur (responsabilidad solidaria).
  • Gümrük müşaviri ücreti yaklaşık 3.500 ile 15.000 MXN arasıdır, ya da mal değerinin yaklaşık yüzde 0,35 ile 0,65'i (camtomx, teyit edildi 2026-07-13).
  • ABD menşeli mallar T-MEC kapsamında çoğu üründe yüzde 0 gümrük vergisine tabidir; STA'sız menşe için oran farklıdır.
  • Menşe belgesi 2026'da sevkiyattan önce dijital yüklenir; yoksa tam üçüncü ülke vergisi uygulanır (trade.gov).

Pedimento nedir, süreç nasıl işler?

Pedimento, Meksika gümrüğünün resmi ithalat kaydıdır. Malın yasal girişini ve vergilerin ödendiğini kanıtlar; her sınır geçişinde lisanslı müşavir tarafından düzenlenir.

Pedimento, Meksika vergi ve gümrük idaresi (SAT) tarafından zorunlu tutulan elektronik beyandır. İçinde malın gümrük değeri, tarife kodu (fracción arancelaria), menşei, ödenen gümrük vergisi ve IVA, taşıma bilgisi ve gümrük müşavirinin kaydı yer alır. ABD'den Laredo üzerinden Meksika'ya ticari gönderi yapıyorsanız süreç şöyle işler: siz ticari faturayı, çeki listesini ve ürün bilgilerini sağlarsınız; lisanslı gümrük müşaviri bu bilgilerle pedimentoyu hazırlar ve SAT sistemine sunar; gümrük vergisi ile IVA ödenir ve pedimento numarası oluşur; mal serbest bırakılır ve iç taşımayla varış deposuna, örneğin Monterrey'e gider. Belge, ürünün Meksika'ya yasal girişinin tek geçerli ispatıdır; muhasebe ve olası bir SAT denetimi için saklanmalıdır. BringGo Ship, Laredo ve Monterrey depoları ve lisanslı gümrük müşaviriyle bu geçişi tek elden yürütür.

Pedimentoda hangi alanlar bulunur?

Pedimento; ithalatçı ve müşavir kimliğini, tarife kodunu, gümrük değerini, menşei ve ödenen vergileri taşır. Bu alanların faturayla birebir tutması gecikmeyi önler.

Bir pedimentoyu okurken bakmanız gereken temel alanlar şunlardır: pedimento numarası ve rejim (ithalat türü), ithalatçının RFC bilgisi, gümrük müşavirinin patente numarası, ürünlerin tarife kodu, gümrük değeri (genellikle CIF esaslı), menşe ülkesi ve ödenen gümrük vergisi ile IVA tutarları. Faturadaki değer, adet ve tanım pedimentoyla birebir uyuşmalıdır; en sık gecikme sebebi bu uyumsuzluktur. Yanlış tarife kodu hem ödenecek vergiyi hem de fiziki muayene (rojo) riskini artırır. Aşağıdaki tablo, pedimento için gereken temel belgeleri ve her birinin işlevini özetler.

Pedimento ve gümrük maliyeti ne kadar?

Maliyet üç kalemden oluşur: müşavir ücreti, gümrük vergisi ve IVA. Oranlar menşee ve ürüne göre değişir; ABD menşeli mallar çoğu üründe yüzde 0 gümrük vergisine tabidir.

Gümrük müşaviri ücreti yaklaşık 3.500 ile 15.000 MXN arasında değişir, ya da mal değerinin yaklaşık yüzde 0,35 ile 0,65'i olarak hesaplanır; yasayla sabit değildir. IVA yüzde 16'dır; kuzey ve güney sınır bölgesinde şartlı olarak yüzde 8 uygulanabilir. Gümrük vergisinde belirleyici olan menşedir: ABD menşeli mallar T-MEC kapsamında çoğu üründe yüzde 0'dır. Ancak 1 Ocak 2026'da yürürlüğe giren kararname, serbest ticaret anlaşması olmayan ülkelerden (Çin, Türkiye ve diğerleri) gelen 1.463 üründe gümrük vergisini yüzde 7 ile 50 arasına çıkardı; kararname 31 Aralık 2026'ya kadar geçerlidir. Türkiye'nin Meksika ile serbest ticaret anlaşması olmadığı için Türk menşeli mallar bu listedeki kategorilerde daha yüksek vergiye tabi olabilir. Kesin oran için ürününüzün tarife kodunu kontrol edin ve sevkiyattan önce güncel SAT tarifesinden teyit edin.

“Quienes introduzcan o extraigan mercancías del territorio nacional destinándolas a un régimen aduanero, están obligados a transmitir a las autoridades aduaneras, a través del sistema electrónico aduanero, en documento electrónico, un pedimento con información referente a las citadas mercancías.”

Meksika Gümrük Kanunu (Ley Aduanera), 36. madde

Tanımlar

  • Pedimento: Pedimento, Meksika gümrüğüne verilen resmi elektronik ithalat beyannamesidir ve lisanslı gümrük müşaviri tarafından hazırlanır.
  • Agente aduanal: Agente aduanal, Meksika'da ithalat beyanını sizin adınıza sunmaya yetkili lisanslı gümrük müşaviridir.
  • IVA: IVA, Meksika'nın katma değer vergisidir ve standart oranı yüzde 16'dır.

Sık sorulan sorular

Pedimentoyu kendim hazırlayabilir miyim?

Hayır. Ticari ithalatta beyanı yalnızca kayıtlı bir gümrük müşaviri sunabilir; 2026 reformu bunu değiştirmedi. Siz faturayı ve ürün bilgilerini doğru sağlarsınız, beyanı müşavir yapar. Değişen tek şey, artık ithalatçının da beyandan ortak sorumlu olmasıdır.

Pedimento numarasını nerede görürüm?

Numara, gümrük müşavirinizin ilettiği pedimento belgesinde yer alır. Bu belgeyi muhasebe kaydı ve olası bir SAT denetimi için saklayın; ithalatın yasal ispatı budur.

RFC olmadan ithalat yapabilir miyim?

Ticari ithalatta genellikle RFC ve ithalatçı kaydı gerekir; 2024'ten beri kurye kanalında da alıcının RFC'si isteniyor. RFC'niz yoksa kayıtlı ithalatçı (IOR) hizmeti veren bir partner üzerinden gönderi yapabilirsiniz.

Menşe belgesi olmazsa ne olur?

T-MEC tercihli tarifesini kaybeder ve tam üçüncü ülke vergisini ödersiniz. 2026'da menşe belgesi sevkiyattan önce dijital olarak yüklenmelidir; sonradan sunmak kabul edilmez.

Gümrük süreci ne kadar sürer?

Belgeler eksiksizse Laredo sınırından geçiş ve pedimento onayı çoğunlukla aynı gün tamamlanır; Monterrey teslimatı dahil toplam süre genellikle 1 ile 2 iş günüdür. Fiziki muayene (rojo) çıkarsa 1 ile 2 gün eklenir.

keywords: qué es un prep center Amazon FBA México
translations.content:
Un prep center es un almacén que recibe tu mercancía y la prepara según las reglas de Amazon FBA: etiquetado, empaque, agrupado y control de calidad, antes de enviarla a la bodega de Amazon. En la frontera con México suma una ventaja clave: hace el etiquetado NOM en español y coordina la aduana en el mismo paso, así el inventario llega listo tanto para Amazon como para el mercado mexicano.

  • Un prep center prepara inventario para FBA: etiquetas, empaque y control de calidad según las reglas de Amazon (Amazon Seller Central).
  • Amazon México está activo y en crecimiento; Amazon invierte cerca de 6 mil millones de dólares en México hacia 2026 (mexicobusiness.news).
  • La mayoría de productos de retail requiere etiquetado NOM en español para entrar a México (NOM-050, NOM-051).
  • Un TIR bien documentado llega de Laredo a Monterrey en 1 a 2 días hábiles (dato operativo).
  • El IVA de importación es del 16 por ciento (SAT, trade.gov).

¿Qué hace un prep center y por qué conviene en la frontera?

Un prep center prepara tu mercancía para las reglas de Amazon antes de que llegue a la bodega: etiqueta, empaca y revisa calidad. En la frontera, además, hace el etiquetado NOM en español y coordina la aduana, así resuelve dos cosas en un solo lugar.

Un prep center, o centro de preparación, es un almacén especializado que recibe tu inventario y lo deja listo para cumplir las estrictas reglas de recepción de Amazon FBA. Eso incluye pegar el código de barras correcto en cada unidad, empacar productos frágiles o líquidos según norma, agrupar sets, poner bolsas de seguridad cuando aplica y revisar que no haya daños. Si algo llega mal preparado a la bodega de Amazon, se rechaza o se cobran cargos, así que este paso protege tu cuenta. Hasta aquí, un prep center sirve igual en cualquier país. Lo que cambia en la frontera con México es que puede resolver, en el mismo lugar, dos capas más: el etiquetado NOM en español que México exige a la mayoría de productos de retail, y la coordinación aduanal para que la mercancía cruce lista. En vez de preparar para Amazon en un sitio y lidiar con la aduana y el NOM en otro, todo ocurre en el mismo punto de la frontera. BringGo Ship opera este modelo desde Laredo y Monterrey, con almacén, etiquetado y preparación del expediente aduanal en una sola operación.

¿Qué servicios incluye normalmente un prep center?

Recepción e inspección, etiquetado de unidades y cajas, empaque según norma de Amazon, agrupado de sets y reenvío a la bodega. En la frontera se añade el etiquetado NOM y el despacho aduanal.

El paquete de servicios típico de un prep center cubre todo el trayecto entre que la mercancía llega y entra a la red de Amazon. Primero, recepción e inspección: se cuenta, se revisa el estado y se documenta lo recibido. Segundo, etiquetado: cada unidad lleva su código FNSKU y cada caja su etiqueta de envío generada en Seller Central. Tercero, empaque según norma: bolsas selladas con advertencia de asfixia, poli para productos que pueden ensuciarse, protección para frágiles. Cuarto, agrupado y kitting cuando vendes sets o paquetes. Quinto, control de calidad para atrapar defectos antes de que lleguen al cliente y generen devoluciones. Sexto, el reenvío a la bodega de Amazon asignada. En un prep center fronterizo se agregan dos servicios propios del mercado mexicano: el etiquetado NOM en español, indispensable para que el producto entre a México y se pueda listar, y el despacho aduanal con agente aduanal, con su pedimento, IVA y, si aplica, arancel. Reunir todo esto en un solo proveedor reduce errores y traspasos, que es donde suelen aparecer los problemas.

¿Cuánto cuesta usar un prep center?

Se cobra por servicio: una tarifa por recepción, por unidad etiquetada o empacada, y por almacenamiento. Lo importante es que el costo sea desglosado y que se compare contra el valor de evitar rechazos y cargos de Amazon.

Los prep centers cobran por servicio realizado, no una tarifa plana, y ahí está la clave para leer un presupuesto. Lo habitual es una tarifa por recepción del envío, un costo por unidad para el etiquetado y el empaque, cargos por servicios especiales como bolsas de seguridad o kitting, y una tarifa de almacenamiento por el tiempo que la mercancía permanece antes de reenviarse. Un buen proveedor desglosa cada línea para que veas exactamente qué pagas. En un prep center fronterizo hay costos adicionales propios de la importación: la tarifa del agente aduanal por el pedimento, el IVA del 16 por ciento sobre el valor en aduana, y el etiquetado NOM. La forma correcta de evaluar el gasto no es solo mirar la tarifa por unidad, sino compararla contra lo que cuesta un error: una caja rechazada por Amazon, cargos por preparación deficiente, o un producto detenido en aduana por falta de etiqueta NOM. Un prep center bien llevado casi siempre cuesta menos que esos problemas, y confirma cada tarifa antes de enviar, junto con las referencias de Seller Central.

¿Por qué la ubicación fronteriza acelera tu inventario?

Porque el inventario se prepara, se etiqueta en NOM y cruza la aduana en el mismo punto, sin traspasos entre proveedores. Desde Laredo, un envío bien documentado llega a Monterrey en 1 a 2 días hábiles.

La ubicación no es un detalle, es lo que decide cuántos días tarda tu inventario en estar disponible. Cuando el prep center está en la frontera, la mercancía entra desde Estados Unidos, se prepara para Amazon, se etiqueta en NOM y se despacha por la aduana en el mismo lugar, sin viajes intermedios ni traspasos entre empresas distintas. Cada traspaso agrega tiempo y riesgo de error, así que eliminarlos importa. Desde Laredo, el puerto interior más activo de Norteamérica, un envío bien documentado llega a Monterrey en 1 a 2 días hábiles, porque el trayecto son unas horas de manejo más la aduana. Eso significa que tu inventario puede pasar de una bodega estadounidense a estar listo en México en cuestión de días, no semanas. Además, tener presencia a ambos lados de la frontera abre opciones: preparar para FBA México, para el modelo NARF que vende inventario de Estados Unidos a clientes mexicanos, o para fulfillment propio dentro de México. keywords: puentes internacionales Laredo Nuevo Laredo carga
translations.content:
De los cuatro puentes internacionales de Laredo, solo dos mueven camión de carga comercial: el World Trade Bridge, o Puente IV, que es el principal y solo maneja carga, y el Puente Colombia Solidaridad, o Puente III. Los otros dos son de pasajeros. El World Trade Bridge concentra cerca del 40 por ciento de todos los cruces de camión de la frontera.

  • Laredo tiene cuatro puentes internacionales, pero solo el Puente III (Colombia Solidaridad) y el Puente IV (World Trade Bridge) mueven camión de carga comercial (Ciudad de Laredo).
  • El World Trade Bridge abrió el 15 de abril de 2000, tiene 8 carriles y solo maneja tráfico comercial (Ciudad de Laredo, TxDOT).
  • El World Trade Bridge concentra cerca del 40 por ciento de todos los cruces de camión de la frontera México-Estados Unidos (transportgeography, TxDOT).
  • Entre los dos puentes comerciales cruzan del orden de 14,000 a 18,000 camiones cargados al día, con picos por encima de 20,000 (Port Laredo, TxDOT).
  • Laredo es el puerto terrestre más transitado de Norteamérica; un TIR llega de Laredo a Monterrey en 1 a 2 días hábiles (WorldCity, dato operativo).

¿Por qué puente cruza la carga en Laredo?

Por el World Trade Bridge, el Puente IV, que es el principal cruce comercial y solo maneja carga, o por el Puente Colombia Solidaridad, el Puente III, el segundo cruce comercial. Los otros dos puentes de Laredo son de pasajeros, así que un camión de carga no cruza por ellos.

Laredo tiene cuatro puentes internacionales, pero para un embarque de carga solo importan dos, y conviene tenerlo claro para no confundir rutas. El Puente I, Gateway to the Americas, y el Puente II, Juárez-Lincoln, son de pasajeros y peatones, así que un camión comercial no cruza por ahí. La carga comercial cruza por el Puente IV, el World Trade Bridge, y por el Puente III, el Puente Colombia Solidaridad. El World Trade Bridge es el principal cruce comercial de Laredo: abrió el 15 de abril de 2000, tiene 8 carriles y maneja únicamente tráfico comercial, y por sí solo concentra cerca del 40 por ciento de todos los cruces de camión de la frontera entre México y Estados Unidos, lo que lo convierte en el cruce de camión de carga más transitado de la frontera sur. El Puente Colombia Solidaridad, que abrió en 1991 sobre la carretera Mines Road y conecta con Colombia, Nuevo León, es el segundo cruce comercial y funciona como válvula de alivio, manejando tanto carga como tráfico no comercial. Entre los dos mueven del orden de 14,000 a 18,000 camiones cargados al día, con picos por encima de 20,000 en días fuertes. Para un embarque, la elección entre uno y otro suele depender de la congestión y de la ruta, y un operador que cruza a diario, como BringGo Ship, sabe cuándo conviene cada puente.

¿Qué diferencia al World Trade Bridge del Puente Colombia?

El World Trade Bridge es el cruce comercial principal, con 8 carriles y solo carga, y concentra el mayor volumen. El Puente Colombia Solidaridad es el segundo cruce comercial, sobre Mines Road, y sirve de alivio cuando el principal se congestiona; maneja carga y tráfico no comercial.

Aunque los dos mueven carga, no son intercambiables sin más, y entender la diferencia ayuda a planear el cruce. El World Trade Bridge, o Puente IV, es la columna vertebral del comercio de Laredo: dedicado exclusivamente a tráfico comercial, con 8 carriles, es por donde pasa la mayor parte de los camiones y donde se concentra el volumen. Su ventaja es la capacidad y la especialización, pero también es donde más se siente la congestión en horas y temporadas pico. El Puente Colombia Solidaridad, o Puente III, está más alejado del centro, sobre Mines Road, y cruza hacia Colombia, en Nuevo León, en lugar de hacia Nuevo Laredo. Maneja carga y también tráfico no comercial, y funciona como válvula de alivio: cuando el World Trade Bridge se satura, mover un embarque por Colombia puede ahorrar tiempo, a cambio de una ruta un poco más larga. Un dato de contexto que conviene citar con cuidado: el World Trade Bridge tiene 8 carriles, no 14; la cifra de 14 carriles que circula en algunas fuentes corresponde a una ampliación que todavía no está construida. Esa expansión está planeada, con un apoyo federal anunciado a inicios de julio de 2026, pero a mediados de 2026 no está operando. Para elegir puente, lo que importa es la congestión del día y la ruta del destino, y ahí la experiencia de cruzar a diario vale más que cualquier regla fija.

¿Qué volúmenes maneja Laredo y por qué importa para tu carga?

Entre los dos puentes comerciales cruzan del orden de 14,000 a 18,000 camiones cargados al día, con picos sobre 20,000. Ese volumen hace de Laredo el puerto terrestre más transitado de Norteamérica, lo que significa transportistas de sobra, cruces frecuentes y tránsitos cortos a Monterrey.

El volumen de Laredo no es un dato de presumir, sino algo que afecta directamente a tu carga. Entre el World Trade Bridge y el Puente Colombia cruzan del orden de 14,000 a 18,000 camiones cargados al día, con picos por encima de 20,000 en jornadas fuertes; conviene manejar esa cifra como un rango, porque varía por dirección y por día. Ese flujo hace de Laredo el puerto terrestre más transitado de Norteamérica, por donde pasa cerca del 40 por ciento del comercio entre México y Estados Unidos. Para un embarque, esa densidad se traduce en tres ventajas concretas. Primero, oferta de transportistas: en un punto con tanto tráfico es fácil conseguir camión y cupo, lo que da mejores precios y flexibilidad. Segundo, frecuencia: los cruces son constantes, así que la mercancía espera menos. Tercero, cercanía: Laredo está a solo unas horas de manejo de Monterrey, el centro industrial y logístico del norte, de modo que un TIR bien documentado llega en 1 a 2 días hábiles. La otra cara de la moneda es la congestión: tanto volumen significa que en horas y temporadas pico, sobre todo el cuarto trimestre, los cruces se saturan, y ahí conviene dar margen y saber cuándo usar el Puente Colombia como alivio. BringGo Ship cruza a diario por Laredo, con bodega en la frontera y en Monterrey, así que aprovecha esta densidad y elige el puente y el momento que menos retrasa tu carga.

translations.excerpt: A plain-English guide to the Mexican pedimento, the fields importers should review, and the supporting documents behind the declaration.

translations.metaTitle: How to Read a Mexican Pedimento: Review It in Three Passes
translations.metaDescription: Learn what a Mexican pedimento is, who prepares it, and how to review importer, classification, origin, value, regime, and tax fields.
translations.content:
What is a pedimento and how do you read one?

Why was this tariff code selected? What evidence supports the country of origin? How was the customs value built? An importer who can answer those three questions understands the core of the entry.

You do not need to memorize every pedimento key. You do need to recognize your company, your products, and the commercial facts. If a line looks unfamiliar, ask before transmission. The most useful broker relationship is not silent. It leaves the importer with a clear record of what was declared and why.

A pedimento is Mexico's electronic customs declaration for commercial imports and exports. It identifies the parties, merchandise, tariff classification, origin, customs value, regime, duties, and supporting records. An authorized customs professional prepares and transmits it, but the importer should still review the business facts. Treating it as a receipt with one amount at the bottom misses the fields that create future audit risk.

What is a pedimento and who prepares it?

The importer provides product, transaction, and registration information to the customs broker. The broker translates that file into the official declaration, attaches or references required digital documents, calculates charges, and transmits the entry through Mexico's customs system. The commercial invoice, bill of lading, origin evidence, permits, and value documents support the filing. They do not become interchangeable simply because they describe the same shipment.

  • Importer and RFC: Legal party responsible · Importer records
  • Tariff code: Classification and controls · Product specifications
  • Origin and export country: Where made and routed · Origin evidence
  • Customs value: Declared valuation basis · Invoice and payment
  • Regime and keys: Legal customs treatment · Commercial purpose
  • Contributions: Duty, IVA, and other charges · Broker calculation

Which mistakes matter most?

Country of shipment is often confused with country of origin. Goods shipped from a US warehouse are not automatically USMCA-origin goods. Product descriptions can also be too vague to support the selected code. Finally, value, currency, Incoterm, and payment evidence may conflict. Mexico's 2026 electronic value controls make those inconsistencies more visible before entry, so the commercial team and broker must use the same facts.

How should an importer review the document?

Compare legal name and RFC first. Then match each line to the invoice, quantities, weights, description, tariff code, origin, and value. Ask why a preference, permit, or tax treatment applies. Keep the final declaration and supporting evidence with the shipment record. We prefer a short pre-filing review for new products. Ten minutes before transmission is cheaper than a correction after release.

Keep a product master sheet

For repeat SKUs, store the approved description, material, use, origin, tariff code, unit value logic, and required permits. Give the broker controlled updates when the product changes. This reduces accidental drift between shipments. It also makes internal review much faster when a buyer or auditor asks what was declared.

Review it in three passes

  1. Match the importer, supplier, invoice, regime, and customs office to the shipment.
  2. Match each product line to quantity, unit, origin, tariff classification, and declared value.
  3. Review duties, VAT, fees, preferences, permits, and attached electronic records.

Do not approve a line because the total looks familiar. A repeated SKU can still carry a changed origin, value, or specification. Keep the approved version with the invoice, payment evidence, classification note, and release record. If a correction is required, preserve both versions and the reason for the change.

The obligation is written into the Customs Law itself, and it is worth reading in the original because it defines both what a pedimento is and how it must be filed:

“Quienes introduzcan o extraigan mercancías del territorio nacional destinándolas a un régimen aduanero, están obligados a transmitir a las autoridades aduaneras, a través del sistema electrónico aduanero, en documento electrónico, un pedimento con información referente a las citadas mercancías.”

Ley Aduanera, Article 36 (Mexico)

Frequently asked questions

Is a pedimento the same as a commercial invoice?

No. The invoice records the transaction. The pedimento is the customs declaration supported by that invoice and other evidence.

Can an importer correct a pedimento?

Corrections may be possible depending on the field and timing, but they can create cost and scrutiny. Prevent the error before filing whenever possible.
